Then I searched package "kexpmv" and found out it was just archived on 21 Nov.

Then, I also have problem with installing former versions of "kexpmv" from https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/kexpmv/. Warning messages are as below:


I was wonder if anyone met the same problem before and how shall I solve it?


It is much appreciated!!! Many thanks in advance!


Gratefully,

Laura

Hi all-I’m phone but:

gfortran is a compiler for the FORTRAN language which is ancient and technical but fast, 
getting the compilers is nontrivial, 
the binaries don’t need compilers, 
the binaries disappear once CRAN archives the package, 
so I saved the binaries to GitHub, 
exact installation instructions for the binaries are on that GitHub page 
which I sent around a day or two ago

The error you got Laura is from trying to install from CRAN where the package no longer exists, the Matzke_binaries GitHub page shows how to install from a downloaded binary. 

-cheers! Nick

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] AICc test between models.
parts: Hi, thanks for the question...

On Wed, Jan 15, 2020 at 8:16 AM JP F <arapa...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello Nick and everyone,

Happy New Year.

I have a question. I recently ran BioGeoBEARS on a dated phylogeny, ran the 6 models and compared their AICc values.

Interestingly enough, the best model and the second best models have close AICc values. But their range estimates are different for some nodes.

I kind of did the comparison between the best model (bayarealike+j) and the second best (divalike+j) the same way the tutorial shows how to do between, for example, diva and diva+j. I did change the degrees of freedom to 3 for both.

So, the example script runs a few model comparisons.

1. Likelihood ratio test. This compares only 2 models, and one must be nested inside the other one, e.g. DIVALIKE is nested inside DIVALIKE+J.  The LRT provides a p-value.  This is the context where "null" and "alternative" models make sense.  If the null model is true, then the more complex model should only get a significant likelihood improvement 5% of the time (at the 5% cutoff).  The logic of this test relies on the fact that, when models are nested, you really have one model, e.g. when j=0, DIVALIKE+J is identical to DIVALIKE.

In the table you pasted, the columns from "LnLalt" to "tail" are about the LRT.


2. AIC. This can compare any number of models, but it provides AIC model weights, rather than p-values.  The model weights basically provide a measure of relative plausibility.  They can be interpreted rather like Bayesian posterior probabilities, BUT the Bayesian-posterior-probabilities interpretation assumes the true model is in the set of models, which is never the case in real life. The philosophy of AIC is against the idea of p-values, so AIC proponents don't promote cutoffs, they just say "all we have is relative measures of probability, these decline smoothly, we should just use the relative measures directly."

3. AICc. This works the same as AIC, but has a correction for small sample-size bias. Use AICc if you have <50 data (species), above that amount AIC and AICc are basically identical.
What I got as a p-value of 0 (zero). Assuming what I did above is correct, it means that both hypotheses of range estimates are plausible, right?

It's not correct. BAYAREALIKE+J is not nested inside of DIVALIKE+J, so the LRT cannot be used, and you cannot get a p-value on the difference.  Also, since both models have 3 free parameters, the difference in the number of free parameters is 0, so the degrees of freedom is 0, which I think means the chi-squared distribution which gives the p-value is undefined, so the p=0 result you got is probably an NA or something.

The main questions here are actually:
1- Can I compare the AICc values between diva and bay models?
2- If yes, what is the proper way to do it?

The example script produces a pairwise comparison table for 3 pairs of nested models, like the one you pasted in.

But is also produces AIC and AICc tables comparing all 6 models together. I would just use the AICc table.

If 2 models differ in their estimate of ancestral ranges, well, uncertainty is a fact of life!  Often people will publish the estimate of history under the single-best AICc model, but if 2 models are close, they could publish both, or publish one and then discuss the places where there is a difference with another plausible model, etc. Another choice is model-averaging the ancestral range estimates, but I wouldn't worry about that until you feel like you understand the basics of AIC etc.

MAKE SURE to CAREFULLY read:

Advice on statistical model comparison in BioGeoBEARS.
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears

BioGeoBEARS mistakes to avoid.
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid
 
Cheers,
Nick
